description: Inspecting and clearing the workspace, controlling display format, managing the search path and the file system, finding and reading documentation, the command-line debugger, profiling and timing tools, and querying the MATLAB installation and the operating system environment.

tools.name: who
tools.description: Lists the names of variables in the current workspace, optionally filtered by a pattern or read from a MAT-file. Use it for a quick overview during interactive work, and with an output argument to get the names programmatically. `whos` gives the same list with sizes and classes.
tools.usage:
who
who var1 var2
who -file filename
who -regexp pattern
C = who(___)

parameters.name: -file
parameters.description: List variables stored in a MAT-file instead of the workspace.

parameters.name: -regexp
parameters.description: Filter names with a regular expression.

parameters.name: global
parameters.description: List global variables.

tools.notes: Inside a function, `who` lists that function's local workspace only. `evalin('base','who')` lists the base workspace from inside a function.

tools.name: whos
tools.description: Lists workspace variables with their sizes, byte counts, classes and attributes such as complex, sparse or global. Use it to find what is consuming memory and to confirm the class of imported data. With an output argument it returns a struct array you can sort and filter.
tools.usage:
whos
whos var1 var2
whos -file filename
whos -regexp pattern
S = whos(___)

parameters.name: -file
parameters.description: Report on variables stored in a MAT-file.

parameters.name: -regexp
parameters.description: Filter names with a regular expression.

tools.notes: The byte counts reported are for the workspace copies only; copy-on-write means two variables sharing data may each be reported at full size. `whos -file` is the cheapest way to see what a MAT-file contains without loading it.

tools.name: clear
tools.description: Removes variables and other items from memory: named variables, all variables, functions and their persistent state, global variables, classes, or the MEX function cache. Use it to free memory and to reset persistent variables while developing. Clearing everything inside a function is usually a mistake, since function workspaces are cleaned up automatically.
tools.usage:
clear
clear name1 name2
clear -regexp pattern
clear all
clear functions
clear global
clear functionName

parameters.name: all
parameters.description: Clear variables, globals, functions, classes and imports.

parameters.name: functions
parameters.description: Clear compiled function code and persistent variables.

parameters.name: global
parameters.description: Clear global variables everywhere.

parameters.name: -regexp
parameters.description: Clear names matching a regular expression.

tools.example:
a = 1; b = 2; temp1 = 3; temp2 = 4;
clear temp1 temp2
who
clear -regexp '^a'
clear myFunction   % resets its persistent variables
clearvars -except b
tools.notes: `clear all` also unloads compiled functions and MEX files, making the next call noticeably slower; plain `clear` or `clearvars` is enough for variables. Putting `clear all` at the top of a script is a common but counterproductive habit.

tools.name: clc
tools.description: Clears the text from the Command Window without affecting the workspace or the command history. Use it at the start of a script run to make new output easy to read. Scroll-back is discarded, so anything you still need should be saved first.
tools.usage: clc
tools.example:
for k = 1:3
    fprintf('line %d\n', k);
end
clc
disp('fresh start')
tools.notes: clc does not clear variables; that is `clear`. It also does not reset the `diary` file, which keeps recording.

tools.name: disp
tools.description: Displays the value of a variable without printing its name or a blank line, which makes output tidier than omitting the semicolon. It handles any type, including structures, tables and objects. Use `fprintf` when you need formatting control and `display` when you want the name shown as well.
tools.usage: disp(X)

parameters.name: X
parameters.description: Any value to display.

tools.example:
disp('Processing complete')
disp(magic(3))
disp(struct('a', 1, 'b', 'two'))
x = pi;
x
disp(x)
disp(table([1;2], ["a";"b"]))
tools.notes: disp of an empty array prints nothing at all, which can make output confusing. For numeric formatting use `fprintf` or `sprintf`, since disp respects the current `format` setting only.

tools.name: format
tools.description: Sets the display format for numeric output in the Command Window, controlling the number of digits shown and the line spacing. It affects display only; the stored values always keep full double precision. Use `format long` when you need to inspect the exact value of a computation.
tools.usage:
format
format style
format('style')
f = format(___)

parameters.name: style
parameters.description: 'short' (default), 'long', 'shortE', 'longE', 'shortG', 'longG', 'shortEng', 'longEng', 'hex', 'rat', 'bank', '+'.

parameters.name: 'compact'/'loose'
parameters.description: Line spacing; 'compact' is removed in newer releases in favour of the Preferences setting.

tools.example:
format short
pi
format long
pi
format shortG
[1e-5 1e5]
format rat
0.75
format
tools.notes: Changing format never changes the stored value, so a result that looks different after `format long` was always that value. `sprintf('%.15g', x)` gives an exact textual representation regardless of the format setting.

tools.name: path
tools.description: Displays or sets the MATLAB search path, the ordered list of folders searched for functions and files. Use it to inspect the current path, to save and restore a path configuration, and to diagnose shadowing problems. Changes made with `path`, `addpath` and `rmpath` last only for the session unless saved.
tools.usage:
path
p = path
path(newpath)
path(oldpath, newFolder)
path(newFolder, oldpath)

parameters.name: newpath
parameters.description: Path string, with folders separated by `pathsep`.

parameters.name: newFolder
parameters.description: Folder to prepend or append to an existing path.

tools.notes: Saving the old path and restoring it in an `onCleanup` object is the safe way for a function to modify the path temporarily. `restoredefaultpath` recovers from a badly broken path configuration.

tools.name: addpath
tools.description: Adds folders to the MATLAB search path, at the beginning by default so they take precedence over existing functions. Use it to make a project's code available, combined with `genpath` to include subfolders. Changes are temporary unless you call `savepath` or add them to a startup file.
tools.usage:
addpath(folderName1, ..., folderNameN)
addpath(folderName, '-begin')
addpath(folderName, '-end')
oldpath = addpath(___)
addpath(___, '-frozen')

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Folder to add; multiple folders can be given or separated by `pathsep`.

parameters.name: '-begin'/'-end'
parameters.description: Add to the front (default) or the back of the path.

tools.notes: Adding at the beginning can shadow MATLAB's own functions, which produces confusing failures; use '-end' when that risk exists. Capturing the returned old path and restoring it in an `onCleanup` keeps a function from polluting the user's environment.

tools.name: rmpath
tools.description: Removes folders from the MATLAB search path. Use it to undo a temporary `addpath` and to resolve shadowing between two versions of a library. Removing a folder that is not on the path produces a warning rather than an error.
tools.usage:
rmpath(folderName)
rmpath(folderName1, ..., folderNameN)
oldpath = rmpath(___)

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Folder or folders to remove; `genpath` output removes a whole tree.

tools.notes: Removing the folder containing the currently running function does not stop it, but later calls will fail. Pair `rmpath` with `addpath` through `onCleanup` so an error does not leave the path modified.

tools.name: genpath
tools.description: Builds a path string containing a folder and all of its subfolders, skipping special folders such as those beginning with @ or + and named private or resources. Use it with `addpath` to add an entire project tree in one call. It returns the string without modifying the path.
tools.usage:
p = genpath(folderName)
p = genpath(folderName, excludeFolders)

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Root folder of the tree.

parameters.name: excludeFolders
parameters.description: Names of subfolders to skip (R2022b and later).

tools.notes: genpath deliberately skips class folders (@Name) and package folders (+name) because MATLAB finds their contents through the parent folder. Adding a huge tree slows down function lookup, so add only what you need.

tools.name: savepath
tools.description: Saves the current search path so it is restored in future MATLAB sessions, writing to pathdef.m in the preferences folder or to a file you name. Use it after configuring a path you want permanently, but prefer a startup script or a MATLAB project for team work. It returns a status code indicating success.
tools.usage:
savepath
savepath(filename)
status = savepath(___)

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: File to write the path definition to.

tools.notes: Saving can fail with status 1 when the installation folder is not writable; save to `userpath` instead. Hard-coding a path into pathdef.m makes environments hard to reproduce, so a `startup.m` that calls `addpath` is usually better.

tools.name: cd
tools.description: Changes the current working folder, or returns it when called with an output argument. Use it sparingly in scripts, because code that depends on the current folder is fragile; absolute paths built with `fullfile` are more robust. Always restore the original folder when a function changes it.
tools.usage:
cd
cd(newFolder)
cd ..
oldFolder = cd(newFolder)

parameters.name: newFolder
parameters.description: Folder to change to; '..' moves up one level.

tools.notes: Capturing the old folder from the output of `cd` and restoring it with `onCleanup` guarantees the working folder is not left changed after an error. Functions that need files next to their own source should use `fileparts(mfilename('fullpath'))` instead of changing folder.

tools.name: pwd
tools.description: Returns the full path of the current working folder as a character vector. Use it to build absolute paths, to report context in log messages, and to save the location before changing folders. It reflects the process working directory, which affects every relative file operation.
tools.usage: folder = pwd
tools.notes: Relative file names in `fopen`, `load` and `save` are resolved against pwd, so a script that assumes a particular working folder breaks when run from elsewhere. `userpath` and `matlabroot` give the user folder and installation folder.

tools.name: dir
tools.description: Lists folder contents, returning a struct array with name, folder, date, bytes, isdir and datenum fields. Wildcards and `**` for recursive search are supported. Use it to enumerate data files for batch processing and to check file sizes and modification times.
tools.usage:
dir
dir(name)
listing = dir(___)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Folder, file name or wildcard pattern; `**` matches subfolders recursively.

tools.notes: The listing of a folder always includes the '.' and '..' entries, which must be filtered out before recursing. Always join `folder` and `name` with `fullfile` rather than assuming files are in pwd.

tools.name: mkdir
tools.description: Creates a folder, including any missing parent folders, and reports success through optional status and message outputs. Use it to prepare output directories in batch pipelines. Creating a folder that already exists succeeds with a warning unless you capture the status output.
tools.usage:
mkdir(folderName)
mkdir(parentFolder, newFolder)
[status, msg, msgID] = mkdir(___)

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Folder to create; intermediate folders are created as needed.

parameters.name: parentFolder
parameters.description: Existing folder in which to create the new one.

tools.notes: Capturing the status output suppresses the 'directory already exists' warning, which is the usual pattern in scripts. `rmdir(folder, 's')` removes a folder and its contents recursively.

tools.name: rmdir
tools.description: Removes a folder, and with the 's' option removes its entire contents recursively. Use it to clean up temporary working directories. The recursive form is irreversible and deletes without confirmation, so build the path carefully before calling it.
tools.usage:
rmdir(folderName)
rmdir(folderName, 's')
[status, msg, msgID] = rmdir(___)

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Folder to remove.

parameters.name: 's'
parameters.description: Remove the folder and all its contents recursively.

tools.notes: Without 's', removing a non-empty folder fails and returns status 0 with an explanatory message. There is no undo and no recycle bin for the recursive form, so never build the path from unvalidated input.

tools.name: copyfile
tools.description: Copies files or whole folders, optionally overwriting read-only destinations with the 'f' flag. Wildcards let you copy groups of files in one call. Use it in build and packaging steps and to archive inputs alongside results.
tools.usage:
copyfile(source, destination)
copyfile(source, destination, 'f')
[status, msg, msgID] = copyfile(___)

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: File, folder or wildcard pattern to copy.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Target file or folder.

parameters.name: 'f'
parameters.description: Force copying over read-only files.

tools.notes: Copying a folder copies its contents into the destination, creating it if necessary. Always check the status output in scripts, since a failure otherwise passes silently when outputs are requested.

tools.name: movefile
tools.description: Moves or renames files and folders, with the same wildcard and force options as `copyfile`. Use it to rename outputs, to organize results into dated folders, and to implement atomic-ish writes by moving a temporary file into place. Moving across file systems copies and deletes.
tools.usage:
movefile(source, destination)
movefile(source, destination, 'f')
[status, msg, msgID] = movefile(___)

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: File, folder or wildcard pattern to move.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: New location or name.

parameters.name: 'f'
parameters.description: Force the move over read-only files.

tools.notes: Writing to a temporary file and then moving it into place avoids leaving a half-written output if the program fails. On Windows, moving onto an open file fails with a permission error.

tools.name: fullfile
tools.description: Builds a platform-correct file path from folder and file name parts, inserting the right separator and collapsing redundant ones. Use it for every path you construct, so that code works on Windows, Linux and macOS alike. It accepts string arrays and cell arrays to build many paths at once.
tools.usage: f = fullfile(filepart1, ..., filepartN)

parameters.name: filepartN
parameters.description: Folder or file name components; one may be an array to build several paths.

tools.example:
fullfile('data', '2025', 'run1.mat')
fullfile(pwd, 'out.csv')
names = ["a.mat", "b.mat"];
fullfile('data', names)
fullfile('a', '', 'b')
tools.notes: Never concatenate paths with `[folder '\' name]`: it breaks on other platforms and duplicates separators. fullfile does not verify that the path exists; use `isfile` or `isfolder` for that.

tools.name: fileparts
tools.description: Splits a path into its folder, file name and extension parts. Use it to change an extension, to find a file's containing folder, and to extract a base name for building related output names. It is purely textual and does not touch the file system.
tools.usage: [filepath, name, ext] = fileparts(filename)

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: Path to split.

tools.example:
[p, n, e] = fileparts('C:\work\data\run1.csv')
outName = fullfile(p, [n '.mat'])
[~, base] = fileparts('/home/u/report.tex');
base
fileparts(mfilename('fullpath'))
tools.notes: The extension includes the leading dot, and a file with no extension returns an empty ext. For a name containing several dots only the last segment is treated as the extension.

tools.name: isfile
tools.description: Tests whether a path refers to an existing file, returning a logical value. Use it as a clear alternative to `exist(name,'file')`, which also matches folders and files anywhere on the search path. It works elementwise on string arrays.
tools.usage: tf = isfile(path)

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: File path or array of paths.

tools.notes: isfile tests the given path relative to the current folder, not the search path, which is usually what you want. Available since R2017b; `isfolder` is the counterpart for directories.

tools.name: isfolder
tools.description: Tests whether a path refers to an existing folder. Use it before creating output directories and before recursing into a path. Like `isfile`, it resolves relative to the current folder rather than the search path.
tools.usage: tf = isfolder(path)

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Folder path or array of paths.

tools.notes: Available since R2017b, replacing the older `isdir`. `exist(name,'dir')` is the pre-R2017b equivalent and returns 7 for folders.

tools.name: tempdir
tools.description: Returns the system temporary folder, the correct place to write scratch files that do not belong in the project. Combine it with `tempname` for unique file names. Use it in tests and in pipelines that create intermediate files.
tools.usage:
t = tempdir
f = tempname
f = tempname(folder)

parameters.name: folder
parameters.description: For `tempname`, the folder in which to generate the unique name.

tools.notes: tempname returns a unique path but does not create the file, so there is a small race window in multi-process use. Files in tempdir may be removed by the operating system at any time, so never rely on them persisting.

tools.name: which
tools.description: Reports which file MATLAB would execute for a given name, and with the '-all' option lists every match in path order. Use it to diagnose shadowing when a function behaves unexpectedly, and to confirm that your version of a function is the one being called. It also reports variables that shadow functions.
tools.usage:
which name
which name -all
p = which(name)
p = which(name, '-all')
which functionName in classFile

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Function, script, class or variable name.

parameters.name: '-all'
parameters.description: List all matches instead of only the first.

tools.example:
which mean
which mean -all
mean = 5;
which mean
clear mean
p = which('readtable')
which myFunction
tools.notes: If `which` reports 'variable', a workspace variable is shadowing the function, which explains errors like 'Index exceeds matrix dimensions' from an ordinary function call. `-all` order reflects path precedence.

tools.name: what
tools.description: Lists the MATLAB-relevant files in a folder, grouped by type: code files, classes, packages, MAT-files, MEX files, MDL files and P-files. Use it to survey an unfamiliar codebase and to check what a toolbox folder actually provides. With an output argument it returns a struct you can process.
tools.usage:
what
what folderName
w = what(___)

parameters.name: folderName
parameters.description: Folder or partial path to inspect.

tools.example:
what
w = what(pwd);
w.m'
numel(w.mat)
what('matlab/elmat')
tools.notes: Unlike `dir`, `what` classifies files by MATLAB role, which makes it a better first look at a code folder. It does not recurse into subfolders.

tools.name: help
tools.description: Displays the help text of a function, class, method or toolbox folder in the Command Window, taken from the leading comment block of the file. Use it for a quick reminder of syntax without leaving the command line. `doc` opens the full documentation page instead.
tools.usage:
help
help name
help className.methodName
text = help(name)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Function, class, method, or folder name.

tools.example:
help fft
help containers.Map.keys
txt = help('sort');
numel(splitlines(txt))
help('graph2d')
tools.notes: Help text comes from the comments immediately after the function line, so documenting your own functions that way makes `help` work for them too. `lookfor keyword` searches the first help line of every file on the path when you do not know the function name.

tools.name: doc
tools.description: Opens the full HTML documentation page for a function, class or toolbox in the Help browser, including examples, argument descriptions and links to related functions. Use it when the terse `help` text is not enough. Called with no arguments it opens the documentation home page.
tools.usage:
doc
doc name
doc className
doc className.methodName

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Function, class or toolbox name.

tools.example:
doc fft
doc datetime
doc matlab.io.matfile
doc
tools.notes: In `-nodesktop` or `-batch` sessions the Help browser is unavailable, so `help` is the only option there. Documentation can be served from the web or from a local installation depending on your preference setting.

tools.name: type
tools.description: Prints the contents of a file to the Command Window, resolving code file names through the search path. Use it to read the source of a function quickly, to inspect small data files, and to confirm what was written to a text file. It is read-only, unlike `edit`.
tools.usage:
type filename
type('filename')

parameters.name: filename
parameters.description: File name, with or without extension; code files are found on the path.

tools.example:
writelines(["a,b"; "1,2"], 'sample.csv');
type sample.csv
type('startup.m')
type linspace
tools.notes: Built-in functions have no readable source, so `type` reports that it is built in. `edit name` opens the file in the Editor instead, and `dbtype` prints it with line numbers.

tools.name: keyboard
tools.description: Pauses execution and gives control to the keyboard, dropping into debug mode with the current function's workspace available at a K>> prompt. Use it as a deliberate breakpoint inside code you are developing. Type `dbcont` to resume or `dbquit` to abandon execution.
tools.usage: keyboard
tools.notes: A stray `keyboard` left in code will hang an automated batch run waiting for input, so remove them before shipping. `dbstop if error` achieves the same inspection without editing the file.

tools.name: dbstop
tools.description: Sets breakpoints: at a line, at a function, or conditionally on errors, warnings, NaN or Inf values. `dbstop if error` is the single most useful debugging command, stopping exactly where an error occurs with the full workspace intact. Breakpoints are listed with `dbstatus` and removed with `dbclear`.
tools.usage:
dbstop in file at location
dbstop in file at location if expression
dbstop if error
dbstop if caught error
dbstop if naninf
dbstop if warning

parameters.name: file
parameters.description: Name of the code file.

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: Line number, or a function or subfunction name.

parameters.name: if expression
parameters.description: Condition evaluated in that workspace; stops only when true.

parameters.name: if error
parameters.description: Stop at any uncaught error.

parameters.name: if naninf
parameters.description: Stop when a computation produces NaN or Inf.

tools.example:
dbstop if error
dbstop in myFunction at 42
dbstop in myFunction at 42 if k > 100
dbstop if naninf
dbstatus
dbclear all
tools.notes: `dbstop if error` does not trigger for errors caught by a try block; use `dbstop if caught error` for those. Breakpoints persist until cleared and are saved per session, not per file.

tools.name: dbstack
tools.description: Displays or returns the current function call stack, with file names, function names and line numbers. Use it in debug mode to see how execution reached the current point, and inside error handlers to log the call path. The '-completenames' option returns full file paths.
tools.usage:
dbstack
dbstack(n)
ST = dbstack
[ST, I] = dbstack(___)
dbstack('-completenames')

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Number of frames to omit from the top of the stack.

parameters.name: '-completenames'
parameters.description: Return full paths instead of names.

tools.notes: Element 1 of the returned struct is the function that called dbstack, so the caller is element 2. `ME.stack` gives the same information for a caught exception.

tools.name: dbcont
tools.description: Resumes execution from a breakpoint until the next breakpoint or the end of the program. It is one of the family of debug commands together with `dbstep`, `dbquit`, `dbup` and `dbdown`. Use it after inspecting the workspace at a breakpoint.
tools.usage:
dbcont
dbstep
dbstep in
dbstep out
dbquit
dbup
dbdown
tools.example:
% at a K>> prompt after hitting a breakpoint:
% dbstep        % execute the next line
% dbstep in     % step into the called function
% dbup          % move to the caller's workspace
% dbcont        % resume
% dbquit        % abandon execution
tools.notes: `dbquit` ends the debug session and abandons the running program, while `dbcont` lets it finish. `dbup` and `dbdown` move between stack frames so you can inspect the caller's variables.

tools.name: profile
tools.description: Starts, stops and reports the MATLAB profiler, which measures how much time is spent in each function and on each line. Use it to find real bottlenecks before optimizing, rather than guessing. The report can be viewed interactively or retrieved as a struct for automated analysis.
tools.usage:
profile on
profile off
profile viewer
profile resume
profile clear
s = profile('info')
profile('on', '-history')

parameters.name: 'on'/'off'/'resume'/'clear'
parameters.description: Control the profiler state.

parameters.name: 'viewer'
parameters.description: Stop profiling and open the interactive report.

parameters.name: 'info'
parameters.description: Return the collected data as a struct.

parameters.name: '-history'
parameters.description: Also record the sequence of function calls.

tools.notes: Profiling adds significant overhead, so relative times matter more than absolute ones. Code running under the profiler does not benefit from some JIT optimizations, which can make short functions look disproportionately expensive.

tools.name: timeit
tools.description: Measures the typical execution time of a function handle, calling it repeatedly and returning the median time with the measurement overhead removed. It is far more reliable than a single tic/toc for short operations. Use it to compare implementations honestly.
tools.usage:
t = timeit(f)
t = timeit(f, numOutputs)

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function handle taking no input arguments.

parameters.name: numOutputs
parameters.description: Number of outputs to request from f.

tools.notes: The function must take no inputs, so capture data in a closure as in the examples. For code that must run first to warm up caches, call it once before timing. `tic`/`toc` remains appropriate for long-running operations.

tools.name: memory
tools.description: Reports memory use and availability for the MATLAB process on Windows, including the largest contiguous array that can be allocated. Use it to diagnose out-of-memory failures and to size batch processing chunks. It is a Windows-only function.
tools.usage:
memory
userview = memory
[userview, systemview] = memory
tools.notes: On Linux and macOS, memory is not available; use `whos` for workspace usage and operating system tools for process totals. Out-of-memory errors often reflect fragmentation rather than total exhaustion, which MaxPossibleArrayBytes reveals.

tools.name: version
tools.description: Returns the MATLAB version number as a character vector, optionally with the release name, build date, or Java and BLAS details. Use it to record the environment in result files and to guard release-dependent code paths. `verLessThan` compares versions conveniently.
tools.usage:
v = version
v = version('-release')
v = version('-date')
[v, d] = version
v = version('-java')

parameters.name: '-release'
parameters.description: Release designation such as '2025a'.

parameters.name: '-date'
parameters.description: Build date.

parameters.name: '-java', '-blas', '-lapack'
parameters.description: Component version details.

tools.notes: Comparing version strings directly is error prone; `verLessThan('matlab', '9.7')` handles the numbering correctly. Release names map to version numbers non-obviously, so test features with `exist` when possible.

tools.name: ver
tools.description: Displays version information for MATLAB and all installed toolboxes, or returns it as a struct array. Use it to check which toolboxes are installed before calling their functions, and to record the environment for reproducibility. A specific toolbox can be queried by its folder name.
tools.usage:
ver
ver toolboxName
v = ver(___)

parameters.name: toolboxName
parameters.description: Toolbox folder name such as 'signal', 'stats', 'images'.

tools.notes: Being installed is not the same as being licensed and available; `license('test', name)` checks the licence and `matlab.addons.installedAddons` lists add-ons. Toolbox folder names differ from display names.

tools.name: computer
tools.description: Returns a code identifying the computer type MATLAB is running on, such as PCWIN64, GLNXA64 or MACA64, plus optional maximum array size and byte order. Use it for platform-specific code paths and for labelling benchmark results. The simpler predicates `ispc`, `isunix` and `ismac` cover most branching needs.
tools.usage:
str = computer
str = computer('arch')
[str, maxsize] = computer
[str, maxsize, endian] = computer

parameters.name: 'arch'
parameters.description: Return the architecture string used for MEX file extensions.

tools.example:
computer
computer('arch')
[c, maxsz, endian] = computer
if ispc
    exe = 'tool.exe';
else
    exe = './tool';
end
mexext
tools.notes: `mexext` gives the MEX file extension for the current platform, which is what you need when locating compiled binaries. Endianness is 'L' or 'B' and matters for `fopen` machine format choices.

tools.name: getenv
tools.description: Reads an operating system environment variable, returning an empty character vector when it is not set. Use it to pick up configuration such as data directories, API endpoints and credentials supplied by the environment rather than hard-coded. `setenv` sets a variable for the MATLAB process and its children.
tools.usage:
value = getenv(name)
setenv(name, value)
setenv(name)

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Environment variable name.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: Value to set; `setenv(name)` sets it to empty.

tools.notes: Variables set with `setenv` affect the MATLAB process and any processes it launches with `system`, but not the parent shell. Reading secrets from the environment is preferable to storing them in code or MAT-files.

tools.name: system
tools.description: Runs an operating system command and returns its exit status and captured output. Use it to call external tools, to query the platform, and to integrate MATLAB into larger pipelines. The '-echo' option streams output to the Command Window as it is produced.
tools.usage:
status = system(command)
[status, cmdout] = system(command)
[status, cmdout] = system(command, '-echo')

parameters.name: command
parameters.description: Command line to execute in the system shell.

parameters.name: '-echo'
parameters.description: Display the output as the command runs.

tools.notes: A non-zero status means the command failed; always check it. Building a command by concatenating unvalidated input is a shell injection risk, so quote arguments carefully. `dos` and `unix` are platform-specific aliases with the same behaviour.
